items.title: Ed Shaughnessy Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] My name is Monk Rowe and we are filming today for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive...

ctx.x: Do they — is the idea of playing Swing new to them in some cases or have they been exposed to that?

Well it would really all depend on the band director. There are some places you go where I would say that that skill hasn’t been developed very well, and there are other places you go where it’s fair. Fair is about the best. I spend 90 percent of my time trying to get people to play jazz time well. I mean I really can’t get into complex things like odd meters or coordination and independence when those are important, because most of the people aren’t grooving. They are not swinging. And if they don’t have that,…
Yeah, so many of the guys have mentioned that there’s not the training ground that there used to be.

items.title: Ed Shaughnessy Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Ed was interviewed in Clinton, New York on April 25, 1998 by Monk Rowe, director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive.

ctx.x: Ed Shaughnessy may be the most recognized drummer in the country. His dynamic playing and vivacious personality have sparked the bands of Jack Teagarden, Benny Goodman, Duke Ellington and George Shearing. A native of Jersey City, Ed’s first playing experience was in the clubs of the flourishing jazz scene on New York’s 52nd Street. In the 50’s he was kept busy in the studios and as a staff drummer with CBS television. As the Tonight Show drummer, Ed became a familiar face with nation-wide audiences and moved to…
Ed was interviewed in Clinton, New York on April 25, 1998 by Monk Rowe, director of the Hamilton College Jazz Archive.
We are filming for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive on the Hamilton campus today. It’s an extreme pleasure for me to welcome Ed Shaughnessy for actually Part Two of our interview series.
